questions.stem: A bag contains 4 red and 6 blue counters. Two counters are drawn without replacement. Given that the first counter is red, what is the probability the second is also red?
questions.explanation: After removing one red, there are 3 red left out of 9 total. P(2nd red | 1st red) = 3/9 = 1/3. Option (a) uses the original probabilities, ignoring that a counter was removed.
P(B | A) = P(A ∩ B) / P(A) = 0.3 / 0.6 = 0.5. This means that given A has occurred, the probability of B is 0.5. Option (d) incorrectly multiplies P(A) × P(A ∩ B).

questions.stem: 100 students were surveyed. 60 passed maths, 50 passed English, 35 passed both. Given a student passed English, what is the probability they also passed maths?
questions.explanation: P(maths | English) = P(maths ∩ English) / P(English) = 35/50 = 7/10. We restrict to the 50 English students and find how many also passed maths. Option (b) divides by maths total instead.

questions.stem: A box has 3 red and 5 white balls. Two balls are drawn without replacement. What is the probability that the second ball is red?
questions.explanation: P(2nd red) = P(1st red) × P(2nd red | 1st red) + P(1st white) × P(2nd red | 1st white) = 3/8 × 2/7 + 5/8 × 3/7 = 6/56 + 15/56 = 21/56 = 3/8. Interestingly, P(2nd red) = P(1st red) = 3/8.

questions.stem: Events A and B are independent with P(A) = 0.4 and P(B) = 0.5. What is P(A | B)?
questions.explanation: For independent events, P(A | B) = P(A) = 0.4. Independence means knowing B has occurred does not change the probability of A. Option (a) computes P(A) × P(B), which gives P(A ∩ B) for independent events.
